defaultRepertoire.doNotMix: Do not combine c3 with an early f4 in the same game. c3 wants a slow d4 center and takes c3 from the knight; the Vienna Gambit needs Nc3 and a fast f4. Together they loosen the kingside (e3 and g1) without either plan working, and he can hit …d5 while your king is still on e1.

openings.name: Ponziani Opening
openings.story: This is your White opening against 1...e5. The move order is 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.c3, then you aim for d4. That's the same c3-and-d4 idea you liked, with the right timing: Nf3 first puts real pressure on e5, then c3 gets the pawn ready to recapture on d4 so you can keep a broad center. 2.c3 right away (the rare Lopez Opening) takes the c3-square from the knight without attacking e5, so most players wait one move. Black's two honest answers are 3...d5, hitting e4 before you castle, and 3...Nf6, hitting e4 with a piece. Against 3...d5 you have a family move that matches the Alapin (take on d5, then d4) and a sharper Ponziani move, Qa4. Against 3...Nf6 you just play 4.d4, which is the whole point of 3.c3. You've already played the Ponziani 263 times as White (52% score, about 70 accuracy), so this is a system you already know at the base — these chapters fill in the plan after the setup.
ideas: The job of 3.c3 is to support d4. Don't forget to actually play d4, or c3 is just a hole on d3.
Against 3...d5, remember the family sister of the Alapin: 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.d4. Qa4 is the extra Ponziani weapon.
Against 3...Nf6, play 4.d4. If he takes on e4, d5 kicks the knight and Nxe5 follows.
Castle before you go hunting with the queen. Qa4 is a special-purpose move against ...d5, not a license for early queen trips.
The g1 knight already eyes e5. If the e-file opens, that knight and a rook on e1 are your attacking tools — open the center vs an uncastled king.
mnemonics: c3 is the trailer hitch, d4 is the trailer. Hitch first, then back up the pawn.
If he hits e4 with ...d5 or ...Nf6, don't panic: that's the book, and you have a prepared answer.
Same idea as the Alapin: c3, then d4, recapture toward the center.

chapters.name: 3...d5 — he hits e4 with a pawn
chapters.structure: This is Black's most principled reply. He strikes in the center before you've castled. You have two good families of answers, and they are related on purpose. 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.d4 is the same idea you play in the Alapin against 2...d5 (take, then d4). It's the easiest to remember. 4.Qa4 is the traditional Ponziani move: it pins the knight, so e4 is no longer hanging, and you threaten e5. After that you still often play d4.
chapters.mnemonic: Against 3...d5, either take and play d4 (the Alapin sister), or pin with Qa4. Don't just leave e4 hanging.
chapters.ideas: Two answers, one idea: keep a pawn in the center and don't lose e4 for free.

themes.If 4.Qa4 Nf6 (Leonhardt): He develops and hits e4. 5.Nxe5 or 5.exd5 are both book; Nxe5 is the direct one.

chapters.name: 3...Nf6 — he hits e4 with a piece (Jaenisch)
chapters.structure: This is the other main line. He doesn't play ...d5; he attacks e4 with the knight. Your answer is the move the whole opening was built for: 4.d4. If he takes on e4, you push d5, kick the c6-knight, and usually take on e5. If he takes on d4, you can push e5 or recapture. The Vukovic Gambit (4.d4 Nxe4 5.d5 Bc5) looks scary — a piece aims at f2 — but you have a prepared answer. 4.d3 is a quieter backup if you want to avoid the sharp stuff; it's book, just less ambitious.
chapters.mnemonic: Against 3...Nf6, play 4.d4. If he takes on e4, d5 then Nxe5.
chapters.ideas: d4 is the point of c3. When he hits e4 with a knight, you hit back in the center, not with a slow d3 unless you choose to.

chapters.name: Sidelines: 3...f5, 3...Be7, 3...Nge7
chapters.structure: Club players (and some books) also try 3...f5 (the Ponziani Countergambit), 3...Be7 (Romanishin), and 3...Nge7 (Réti). You do not need a new opening. The answer is almost always d4 — the same move — with one extra idea against ...f5.

chapters.ideas: Sidelines don't change the plan. They just change how fast you get d4 in.

openings.name: Sicilian Defence, Alapin Variation
openings.story: This is your White opening against the Sicilian. 1.e4 c5 2.c3, then you want d4. It's the same c3-and-d4 idea as the Ponziani, used on move two because 2.Nf3 would invite all the Open-Sicilian theory you don't need. Against 1...c5, 2.c3 is a real, respected opening (ECO B22), and it's one of the best low-theory weapons you can play. Black's two main replies are 2...d5 and 2...Nf6. Against 2...d5 you already know the pattern from the Ponziani: 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.d4. Against 2...Nf6 you play 3.e5, kick the knight, then d4. Other tries (2...e6, 2...d6, 2...g6) still meet d4.
ideas: 2.c3 prepares d4. Don't get distracted into a Smith-Morra (2.d4 cxd4 3.c3) unless you later choose that on purpose.
Against 2...d5, take and play d4 — the same pattern as Ponziani 3...d5 4.exd5 Qxd5 5.d4.
Against 2...Nf6, 3.e5 Nd5 4.d4. You kick the knight, then build the center.
Against 2...e6, play 3.d4 and you can land in a French Advance where c3 is already on the board.
Castle, then use the open lines. The c-file and the d4-pawn are your middlegame landmarks.
mnemonics: c3, then d4. If he plays ...d5, take then d4. If he plays ...Nf6, e5 then d4.
It's the Ponziani's cousin: same hitch, different first black pawn.

chapters.name: The idea: 2.c3, then d4
chapters.structure: Against the Sicilian you play c3 on move two, because there is no e5-pawn for a knight to attack. Then the plan is d4, and you recapture with the c-pawn when you can, keeping a broad center instead of the Open Sicilian's open c-file mess.

chapters.ideas: This is the trunk of the Alapin. The next chapters are just 'what he tries instead of letting you have d4 for free.'

themes.If 2...d6 or 2...g6: Still 3.d4. Don't invent a new system.

chapters.name: 2...d5 (Barmen) — take, then d4
chapters.structure: This is the most common club try and the closest cousin of Ponziani 3...d5. You take on d5, his queen comes out, and you play d4. After that: develop Nf3, Be2 or Bd3, O-O, and kick the queen later with c4 or Nc3. If he takes on d4, recapture with the c-pawn.

chapters.ideas: Remember it as the same sentence as the Ponziani sister: take on d5, then d4.

openings.name: The c3 and d4 family (vs French, Caro, Scandinavian)
openings.story: Your White repertoire is one idea, used with the right timing against each of Black's first moves. The idea is a pawn on c3 that supports a pawn on d4, so when the center opens you recapture toward the middle and keep a broad, easy-to-play center. Against 1...e5 that's the Ponziani (Nf3 first, then c3, then d4). Against 1...c5 that's the Alapin (c3 on move two, then d4). Against 1...e6 (French) you play 2.d4 d5 3.e5 and 4.c3 — the Advance — which is the same hitch already on the board. Against 1...c6 (Caro-Kann) you play 2.d4 d5 3.e5, the Advance, and c3 often appears a move or two later when he plays ...c5. The Exchange with 3.exd5 cxd5 4.Bd3 and c3 is a simpler cousin if you want less theory. Against 1...d5 (Scandinavian) you do not play an early c3, because his queen is sitting on d5 and 3.Nc3 is the move that gains a tempo. You still play d4 right after. The family idea here is the broad center, not the c3-pawn itself. That's the one sentence to remember: c3 supports d4 except when a knight on c3 does the job better, which is really only the Scandinavian.
ideas: One idea, right timing: c3 supports d4 against 1...e5 (Ponziani) and 1...c5 (Alapin).
Against the French, 3.e5 and 4.c3 is the same structure — a space advantage with a solid d4-pawn.
Against the Caro-Kann, 3.e5 is the main choice; c3 appears when he plays ...c5. The Exchange plus c3 is the quieter backup.
Against the Scandinavian, 3.Nc3 then d4 — don't play early c3, because kicking the queen is more important.
When the center opens, recapture toward the middle, castle, then attack. Open the center vs an uncastled king; don't go queen-hunting first.
mnemonics: c3 is the hitch, d4 is the trailer — except vs the Scandinavian, where Nc3 kicks the queen and d4 still comes.
French and Caro Advances are the same house: e5, d4, and a c-pawn that can support d4.

chapters.name: Against 1...d5: take, kick the queen, then d4
chapters.structure: The Scandinavian is the one place you should not play an early c3. After 1.e4 d5 2.exd5 Qxd5, 3.Nc3 gains a whole tempo on the queen. 3.c3 would be too soft — the hitch isn't needed when a knight can do a better job. openings.name: Scotch and Petrov
openings.story: This is the family you asked about. After 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3, Black has two different jobs, and 3.d4 means something slightly different in each one. If he plays 2...Nc6, he is developing and defending e5 — that's the road into the Scotch (3.d4). If he plays 2...Nf6, he is not defending e5; he is counterattacking your e4-pawn — that's the Petrov (Russian Defence). 3.d4 against the Petrov is the Modern Attack, which you called the Modern Scotch. The two lines really do look alike, and that's why they're hard to tell apart: both open the center with d4, but the extra knight is on a different square, so the answers change. This opening's job is to make those situations sit next to each other, with the same ideas labelled the same way. You used to play the Scotch and felt buried by the branches. Here the branches are grouped by what he is trying to do, not by a long list of move-orders. The London is still your everyday White system; this chapter is here so the open games stop feeling like a maze.

If he grabs on e4 (3...Nxe4 in the Petrov), don't panic: Bd3 and development first, then take or pressure e4/e5.
An early ...Qh4 in the Scotch is a queen raid. Don't chase it forever — develop, threaten, and look at Nb5.

openings.name: London System
openings.story: The London System is a setup opening. You put the same pieces on the same squares almost every game: pawns on d4, e3 and c3 (the 'pyramid'), the dark-squared bishop on f4 — outside the pawn chain, before you close it — then Nf3, e3, Nbd2, Bd3 and kingside castling. Because the plan doesn't change much when he tries a different defence, you can learn the ideas once and reuse them, instead of memorizing a new tree every time he deviates (the problem you ran into in the Scotch). The typical middlegame plans are Ne5, a kingside attack with the bishop pointing at h7, or the e4 break once you're fully developed. Club players often answer 1.d4 with ...d5; the London is built for that, and it also handles ...Nf6, ...c5 and ...g6 without a theory explosion.

If he plays ...c5 and ...Qb6, you can often ignore the b2 pawn (or play Qb3) and keep developing.

openings.name: Pirc Defence (and the Modern setup vs non-e4)
openings.story: The Pirc starts 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6, then ...Bg7 and usually ...O-O. The setup is easy; the work is the attacking plan after it, and that depends on what White does. This opening is also your answer to 1.d4, 1.c4, 1.b4 and 1.g3: the same g7 bishop, then a break with ...e5 or ...c5. The Fianchetto module covers how to use that bishop and how to time the h-pawn against flank openings.
ideas: The bishop on g7 is the key piece. Open its diagonal with a pawn trade (...e5 or ...c5), don’t sit behind a closed wall.
Against the Austrian (4.f4): ...c5 or ...e5 after you castle, and be ready for a fight.
Against the 150 Attack (Be3+Qd2): if he castles queenside, push the a- and b-pawns and use the g7 bishop against his king. You can also delay ...O-O and play ...c6, ...b5.
Against the Classical (Nf3+Be2): ...e5 or ...c5, then ...Nc6 and ...Re8, and attack on the side your pawns point.
Against 4.g3, treat it like a kingside fianchetto: take a share of the center, then the usual breaks.

openings.name: Caro-Kann Defence
openings.story: The Caro-Kann starts with 1...c6 and 2...d5. You challenge his e-pawn the same way the French does, but you keep the door open for the light-squared bishop. That's the whole point: in the French the bishop is often stuck on c8; in the Caro you develop it to f5 or g4 before you play ...e6. At the 1000–1400 level you will mostly see 3.exd5 (the Exchange), 3.e5 (the Advance), and 3.Nc3 or 3.Nd2 (the Classical). Many 1.e4 players all open 1.e4 a lot, so this is your regular answer to the king's pawn. The middlegame plans are solid: a strong point on d5, a minority attack or ...c5 break in the Exchange, and a safe king after you castle. You don't need to memorize every Advance sideline on day one — learn the Short System ideas first, then add the sharper ones.

openings.name: Queen's Gambit Declined
openings.story: Against 1.d4 you play 1...d5 and meet the Queen's Gambit (2.c4) with 2...e6, the Queen's Gambit Declined. You hold the center, develop the knights to f6 and c6 or d7, the bishop to e7, and castle. The light-squared bishop is the one problem child — just like in some of your own games — so the recurring job is to free it with ...b6 and ...Bb7, or with a later ...dxc4 and ...c5 / ...e5. 1.d4 shows up as well as 1.b4 and 1.g3; this chapter also covers his other queen's-pawn tries: the London (2.Bf4), the Colle (2.e3 or 2.Nf3 and e3), and the Veresov or Jobava (early Nc3 and Bf4). Don't meet 1.d4 with the Englund (1...e5). That's a trap-hunting opening and it doesn't fit this repertoire.
ideas: Against 1.d4 play 1...d5. Against 2.c4 play 2...e6, then ...Nf6, ...Be7, and castle.

Against the London, Colle, or Jobava, you can still play a ...d5 / ...e6 / ...Nf6 / ...Be7 setup — the same house, a different roof.
mnemonics: Hold d5, castle, then free the light-squared bishop.

openings.name: Against 1.b4 (Polish / Sokolsky)
openings.story: The Sokolsky / Polish Opening is A common first move in your games (25 of his White games in your head-to-head). He also plays it often in public games. The easy, theoretical answer is 1...d5. You take the center, develop with ...Nf6, ...e6 or ...Bf5, ...Be7, and castle. The one rule that will save you games: don't hunt the b4 pawn too early. The pawn is a bait. If you grab it before you're developed, his bishop on b2 and a rook on b1 often get there first. After you castle, the middlegame looks like a Queen's Gambit or a London-in-reverse: a solid center, a safe king, and a later ...c5 or ...e5 break.

openings.name: Against 1.g3 (King's Fianchetto / KIA)
openings.story: 1.g3 is Another common try in your games (24 head-to-head games) and his most common White first move in public games. He fianchettoes, often transposes into a King's Indian Attack or a Réti, and hopes you wander with an early ...h5–h4 raid. Don't. The reliable answer is again 1...d5, then ...Nf6, ...e6 or ...c6, ...Be7, and castle. After that you can play ...c5 or ...c6 and a later ...e5, depending on where he puts his pawns. If he transposes into a regular 1.d4 or 1.c4 position, you already know the QGD / ...d5 structures.
